extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors querying agents and prospective literary-agency interns
extracted.subtask_description: Practical tips for preparing and sending queries/manuscripts to literary agents and for working as an intern at a literary agency. Covers submission mechanics, what agents/interns look for, and basic industry best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font choice / readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Easy on the font. Use Times New Roman or a clear serif.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard, highly readable fonts for submissions; avoid decorative or unusual typefaces that distract or reduce readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone of reader's report
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing your reader’s report, watch the tone. You’re trying to help the writer improve his or her story, so it’s important to maintain a cordial tone throughout your report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide constructive criticism framed helpfully; avoid overly harsh or dismissive language. Aim to identify strengths and weaknesses while remaining professional and supportive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't announce additional manuscripts when submitting one
rubrics_metrics.description: When submitting one novel, don’t mention that you have another one in the works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent really likes your writing, he or she will ask about other projects. Mentioning other works up front can signal lack of confidence or look like unnecessary noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research agent genre/availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Research your potential agent. Did you write a YA novel? Check if she or he is accepting queries for that genre at the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm an agent's current interests and submission windows before querying to avoid wasting time and to increase chances of a positive reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell your supervisor what you like to read (intern networking tactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let your supervisor know what you like to read. I told my supervisor that I love reading literary fiction, so he would always send me those queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an intern, communicate your preferences to get experience relevant to your interests; this can influence the work you are assigned and what you learn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Queries are first impressions that agents get of clients, so proofread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully proofread query letters; typos and careless errors harm credibility and first impressions. Ensure grammar, spelling, and formatting are clean.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mass-emailing agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Never send a mass email. Always address one agent at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalize each query to the specific agent; avoid blanket messages that show no research or care about fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid telling origin anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t mention how you got your novel idea. Agents don’t care if God told you to write something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit irrelevant origin stories or sensational explanations for your idea; focus on the book and your credentials instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a detailed synopsis ready
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a detailed synopsis ready in case the agent likes what you’ve sent him/her so far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a concise, complete synopsis (covering plot arc, ending, and main characters) so you can promptly provide it upon request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't compare yourself to literary greats
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t compare your writing style to legendary writers like Ernest Hemingway or Jane Austen. That’s just pompous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grandiose or presumptuous comparisons in queries; let your writing speak for itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontload story — first ten pages matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The first ten pages matter. They usually tell agents to read more. You might be asked to submit a partial (50 pages) or a full manuscript. So, it’s important that you get to the point of your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the opening pages establish momentum, character, and stakes; avoid long, slow setups that lose an agent’s interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow agency submissions guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the literary agency’s submissions guidelines. It’s that simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere precisely to stated formatting, materials requested, and submission processes on an agency's website to avoid automatic rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include relevant writing experience in query
rubrics_metrics.description: Include relevant writing experience in your query. If you’re writing mystery and you’re a member of a mystery writing club, let them know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight credentials, memberships, publications, or experience that demonstrate domain knowledge or writing practice relevant to your manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform expectations by nonfiction type
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re writing prescriptive nonfiction, have a platform. If you’re writing narrative nonfiction, you have to write well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that prescriptive/how-to nonfiction typically requires an author platform (audience, credentials), while narrative nonfiction competes on literary quality and storytelling craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interns: take books from the book pile
rubrics_metrics.description: Interns: Take books from the book pile. Book piles are heaps of gold. Don’t pass up an opportunity to get FREE books (and no late fees from the library).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an intern, use available resources (office book piles) to read widely and learn; treat them as learning opportunities and freebies when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep up with publishing-industry news
rubrics_metrics.description: Know what’s going on the publishing industry. I recommend reading PubTalk, Galley Cat, Mediabistro – any site that relates to publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly read industry blogs and news sites to stay informed about trends, deals, and changes that affect submissions and agent interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network / make friends in publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Make friends, because you’ll never know what’s going to happen two years, three years, etc. down the line. Publishing peeps are fun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate professional relationships; networking can create future opportunities and insider knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query evaluation focuses: narrative momentum, character, marketability
rubrics_metrics.description: If I liked a query, I would say so (two paragraphs talking about narrative momentum, character, marketability – all things to consider when reading a manuscript), and then I’d get either a partial manuscript (50 pages) or a full manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a query, assess the story's narrative momentum, the strength and depth of characters, and the book's marketability; positive assessment leads to requests for partial (≈50 pages) or full manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's report for full manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: For a full script, I would have to write a one-page reader’s report listing the story’s strengths and weaknesses and a suggestion as to whether or not the agent should represent the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concise, one-page reader’s report should summarize key strengths and weaknesses and give a clear recommendation about representation; be specific and evidence-based where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research prize winners / potential novelists
rubrics_metrics.description: I’d also research recent literary prize winners and see if their work could become a novel or if they’re already at work on a novel (making sure, of course, that they are not already represented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents/interns should track prize winners and potential clients, checking whether short-form authors might be converting to novels and whether they lack representation.
